I. INTRODUCTION
The stability of conventional power systems depends on
effective frequency and voltage regulation, traditionally provided by synchronous generators (SGs). As inverter-interfaced
sources increasingly replace SGs, it becomes essential for
these inverters to assume similar regulation capabilities [1]. Grid-forming (GFM) control offers a promising solution,
enabling a wide range of inverter-based systems, including
photovoltaics (PVs) [2], wind turbines [3], railway systems
[4], and charging stations [5], to support grid stability. From a control architecture perspective, GFM control can
be categorized into single-loop GFM (SL-GFM) [5] and multiloop GFM (ML-GFM) structures [2]. Furthermore, on the AC
side, GFM control typically includes an active power (AP)
loop and a reactive power (RAP) loop.

the AP loop, addressing frequency-related interactions, and
proposing methods to improve frequency support. In contrast,
stability issues associated with the RAP loop have received
comparatively little attention [8].

stability issues associated with the RAP loop have received
comparatively little attention [8]. Meanwhile, in the stability
of SL-GFM control, power loops and LCL resonance are typically treated as decoupled due to their different bandwidths,
often leading to the neglect of LCL dynamics [9]. Most existing research on LCL resonance focuses on conventional grid-following (GFL) control [10]–[12], where instability can arise when the current loop, combined with LCL
dynamics, results in an insufficient stability margin according
to the 0dB gain and −180◦phase crossover criteria of the Bode
plot [13]. Recently, limited studies have been extended to GFM
control, with findings indicating that LCL resonance stability
in GFM is strongly influenced by the filter capacitor, which
affects the LCL resonant frequency [6], [14].

in GFM is strongly influenced by the filter capacitor, which
affects the LCL resonant frequency [6], [14]. However, the role
of power loops remains insufficiently explored. Our previous
work identified that when the RAP loop uses droop-I control,
open-loop instability may occur, impacting LCL resonance
stability even when their bandwidths are well separated [15]. This limits the direct use of traditional Bode plot criteria. However, such instability has primarily been analyzed through
root-locus methods, which are dependent on specific parameter
values. This paper presents a detailed investigation of the openloop unstable behavior in the SL-GFM structure with droop-
I control in the RAP loop.

It is observed from Fig. 3 and (46) and (47) that, in
the absence of voltage magnitude feedback of V, the openloop poles are precisely at the system’s natural resonance
frequencies ω1, ω2, and ωg by letting det(A)det(B) = 0. These
poles lie on the imaginary axis, indicating marginal stability. In
practical systems, the presence of parasitic resistances causes
these poles to shift into the left-half plane (LHP), ensuring that
the power loops remain minimum-phase. Consequently, the 0
dB gain and -180◦phase crossover conditions of the Bode
plot criteria can be reliably used to assess system stability
margins. However, when the voltage magnitude ∆V is included
in the feedback branch of the RAP loop, the situation changes
fundamentally.

V. CONCLUSION
This paper investigates the open-loop instability observed
in SL-GFM control. By applying Routh’s Stability Criterion,
the root cause of this instability is analytically identified as a
structural issue arising from the feedback of the voltage magnitude. Consequently, the RAP loop becomes strongly coupled
with the system’s resonant dynamics, and conventional Bode
plot-based crossover criteria are insufficient without explicitly
accounting for these unstable open-loop poles. The findings
underscore that the SL-GFM converter with droop-I control
should be used with caution and only when resonant instability
is explicitly addressed.

or SL-GFM with droop control. The findings in Section II-B suggest a need for further
analysis of the RAP loop using the detailed model.

III. ACTIVE DAMPING STRATEGY
From the perspective of the CL frequency characteristics, the resonance implies that the system contains resonant
peaks around the resonant frequencies. The resonance not
only influences the high-frequency stability of the system
but also deteriorates the power quality by amplifying disturbances/noises around these resonant frequencies. Therefore,
proper AD designs are required to provide sufficient damping. A. Selection of Active Damping Implementation
Ideally, AD introduces a virtual resistor in one of six
possible locations, labeled Rv1 to Rv6 in Fig. 17. As discussed
in [18], all virtual resistors can be implemented using feedback
from iabc, igabc, icabc, or vabc, leading to 24 possible AD
configurations.

paper_title: LCL Resonance Analysis and Damping in Single-Loop Grid-Forming Wind Turbines
text:

in [18], all virtual resistors can be implemented using feedback
from iabc, igabc, icabc, or vabc, leading to 24 possible AD
configurations. Although the AD strategies based on hybrid
feedback variables may improve the robustness by offering
additional control degrees of freedom, it inevitably increases
the complexity of both the structure and the parameters tuning
[27]. Therefore, when resonance can be effectively suppressed,
the AD strategy usually uses the single-variable feedback
scheme. For GFL converters, igabc feedback to implement Rv4
has been identified as the most suitable approach in terms of
number of sensors, implementation complexity, and damping
effectiveness. However, applying these same selection criteria

will be discussed in this section.
1) Number of Sensors: For SL-GFM converters, both igabc
and vabc are measured for power calculation. Therefore, the
AD should be implemented using only these variables whenever possible, avoiding additional sensors. This requirement
leads to 12 possible implementations.
2) Complexity: Using igabc results in controllers where the
order of the numerator is higher by at least two than that
of the denominator. The same applies when constructing Rv1,
Rv3, or Rv6 with vabc [18]. These choices are not favorable
in practice due to implementation complexity.

paper_title: Equivalence of Virtual Synchronous Machines and Frequency-Droops for Converter-Based MicroGrids
text:
I. INTRODUCTION
A
“Virtual Synchronous Machine” (VSM), labeled as
“VISMA,” was ﬁrst presented in English by Beck and
Hesse in 2007 [1]. Later, the VSM concept for emulating
the behavior of synchronous machines (SMs) by controlling
voltage source converters (VSCs) has been pursued by several
other authors [2]–[4]. In the future perspective of decentralized
generation with increasing penetration of converter-interfaced
energy sources, VSMs are being recognized as an effective
method for addressing potential stability issues by adding
virtual inertia to the power system.
In the adjacent research area of converter-dominated microgrids, droop-based schemes have become the preferred solution for control of VSCs [5]. These control schemes can ensure stand-alone operation and load sharing among parallel connected VSC units both in steady state and during transients, similarly to what is achieved with traditional SMs.
The VSM and the droop-based schemes have emerged almost
independently and in two separate contexts, but present strong
similarities. In fact, the two approaches are equivalent under
certain conditions, as proven in this letter.

not change the overall behavior of the VSM, but only introduces small additional oscillations superimposed to the inertial

paper_title: Equivalence of Virtual Synchronous Machines and Frequency-Droops for Converter-Based MicroGrids
text:
V. CONCLUSIONS
This letter has demonstrated the equivalence between
VSM-based control and frequency-droop controllers. The
demonstrated equivalence links into a single theoretical frame
two well established concepts that have been developed so
far in separate contexts. This provides a new perspective for
the VSM and a deeper physical insight into the interpretation
of the gain and ﬁlter parameters for droop controllers in converter-based microgrids.

I. INTRODUCTION
As power systems move towards a larger share of renewable
energy sources, more inverter-based resources (IBRs) replace
traditional generation interfaced via synchronous machines
(SMs), creating new challenges to the understanding of system
stability, and dynamic behavior [1]. There have been significant efforts to understand the effects of control strategies
of IBRs on system stability, e.g., grid-following (GFL) and
grid-forming (GFM) using quasi-static Phasors (QSP) and
electromagnetic transients (EMT) approaches. Recent studies
have uncovered interactions between excitation systems and
inverter controllers using small-signal analyses [2], as well as
effects of QSP network modeling in the global and smallsignal stability of GFM inverters [3], [4].

V. CONCLUSIONS
This paper demonstrates that small-signal stability conclusions for IBRs are heavily dependent on modeling assumptions
regarding electromagnetic network phenomena and load representation. The results indicate that common load modeling
practices need to be revisited for future dynamic studies in
the presence of IBRs. As power systems integrate increasing
amounts of electronics-based loads that behave as CPLs and
IBRs, more advanced models are needed to assess stability.
However, we have only explored single-line systems and a
specific set of parameters and load models. More comprehensive studies are needed using composite load models in more
extensive systems to properly assess the changing stability
regions as we increase system loading. Future work should
focus on understanding real load dynamics by exploring different load composition scenarios and using a combination
of SMs and IBRs controls in the system, while studying
parameter tuning on their controls to enhance stability. Further,
the inclusion of limiters for SMs controllers and current limits
in IBRs can significantly affect system stability and introduce
limit-induced bifurcations. Exploring more precise control and
protection effects in IBR-dominated systems in combination
with load recovery models is also a relevant research direction.

2. Power electronic converters
Advances in semiconductor technology and energy-conversion efficiencies of power electronic converters (PECs) during the last few
decades have resulted in the widespread adoption of PECs at various
levels of the power system. At the consumer level, PECs are generally
deployed in the form of DC-to-DC converters for general electronic
devices, or AC-to-DC converters for laptops, computers, and televisions,
to name a few. Large-scale PECs, such as rectifiers and inverters, are
generally used to control the flow of tens of kilowatts to hundreds of
megawatts (or the reactive power equivalent) of power. At the power
transmission level, PECs typically interface variable and uncertain renewable sources, such as solar PV, with the AC power system, resulting
in an asynchronous generation source.

in an asynchronous generation source. The increased integration of
renewable energy sources into the power system consequently leads to
increased PEC penetration, both from an annual energy and instantaneous perspective. PECs have a wide range of applications, and they can generally be
categorized into the following groups:
• AC-to-DC converters (rectifiers)
• DC-to-AC converters (inverters)
• DC-to-DC converters
• AC-to-AC converters
In this paper, the conversion of interest is DC to AC because the
emphasis is on IBRs, which interface the solar PV DC source with the AC
power system. Therefore, in the following sections, the terminology
relating to PECs, in general, also refers to IBRs.

2.1. Power electronic fundamentals
Central to PECs are semiconductor devices operating in switched
mode. In other words, electronic switches are realized using diodes and
transistors. In addition to diodes and transistors, PECs employ static
devices, including inductors, capacitors, and transformers. An integral
part of each PEC is the control system, which is necessary to achieve the
desired output and efficiency. Fig. 6 shows a diode, which is a two-terminal semiconductor device;
and a transistor, which is a three-terminal semiconductor device.

and efficiency. Fig. 6 shows a diode, which is a two-terminal semiconductor device;
and a transistor, which is a three-terminal semiconductor device. Unlike
the transistor, whose conduction stage depends on an externally applied
signal at the controlled terminal (gate, G), the diode is a passive
switching element, which means that its conductivity is determined by
the applied voltage and current. The diode allows current to flow in one
direction—from the collector (anode) to the emitter (cathode)—while
blocking current in the opposite direction. When the collector terminal
(C) is at a higher potential than the emitter terminal (E), the switch is
closed and the current flows in the direction indicated by i. This current
flow causes a voltage drop from C to E known as a diode’s forward
voltage drop.

Solar PV inverters are used for both stand-alone and grid-tied systems.

2.2. Basic operation
Solar PV inverters are used for both stand-alone and grid-tied systems. Solar PV panels produce DC power, which must be converted to
AC power to interface with the power system, a process that is accomplished with the inverter. Inverters (or charge controllers, depending on the Solar PV interfacing scheme) commonly incorporate
maximum power point tracking control schemes to achieve optimal
energy production, either directly for the DC-to-AC conversion, or while
charging a battery system. The AC output current generated by the
inverter must have the same frequency and maintain a specified relative
phase with the utility grid AC voltage waveform (60 Hz in the United
States) to accomplish the desired power injection into the power
system.

relative
phase with the utility grid AC voltage waveform (60 Hz in the United
States) to accomplish the desired power injection into the power
system. The topology of the basic, single-phase inverter is based on the fullbridge, high-frequency IGBT module (Fig. 7). This topology consists of
four semiconductor switches: four IGBTs with four diodes in antiparallel, two on each branch. The semiconductors of each branch are
complementary in performance, which means that when one is switched on, the other is switched off, and vice versa. The fraction of time
during which a switch pair is in the on state within one switch cycle is
called a duty cycle, with output voltage of the inverter a function of the
duty cycle. Adjusting the duty cycle in a periodic manner is a control
strategy known as PWM.

2.3. Control
An integral part of each solar PV IBR is the closed-loop control
system, which ensures proper inverter operation with high efficiency. Fig. 9 illustrates the basic layout of grid-connected solar PV inverter
arrays with a multilevel control scheme, assuming the basic solar PV
inverter shown in Fig. 7. The control system typically consists of three

Initially, the majority of grid connected solar PV inverters were
controlled to inject whatever power was currently available (grid-parallel inverters). However, with improved control schemes and grid
codes, the general class of grid-supporting inverters has grown more
common. Grid-supporting inverters modulate active and reactive power
set points in order to support grid stability. A standard mode of operation for grid supporting operation is open loop droop control based
on the active power-frequency (P-f) and reactive power-voltage (Q-V)
coupling characteristics in AC transmission systems.

3. Power system stability
Power system stability is a large field rich in mathematics and firmly
grounded by the physics of power system devices, in particular SMCs,
which has traditionally focused on three domains of stability: rotor
angle, frequency, and voltage (Kundur et al., 2004). At high instantaneous penetrations, solar IBRs can introduce challenges for the
stable operation of power systems. This section discusses these traditional stability domains as well as the anticipated or identified impacts
from high IBR penetrations by reviewing recent stability research with
high levels of IBRs. Additionally, system strength and fault response are
discussed through the lens of high IBR penetration levels.
3.1.

high levels of IBRs. Additionally, system strength and fault response are
discussed through the lens of high IBR penetration levels.
3.1. Measuring stability
Although it is impossible to fully partition the rotor angle, frequency, or voltage domains from each other, doing so is a standard
practice that readily simplifies the approach in determining stability
and aids in identifying mitigating measures (Kundur et al., 2004). In
this section, we briefly review these three measures of stability, and the
next section discusses how IBRs have been shown to impact these metrics in recent stability studies with high IBR penetrations. Additional
review material is provided and referenced in Appendix A.
3.1.1.

review material is provided and referenced in Appendix A.
3.1.1. Rotor angle
Rotor angle stability is the ability of the connected and synchronized SMCs (or more generally, generation sources) to maintain rotor
angles within stable boundaries following a perturbation, with no
persisting oscillations (Kundur et al., 2004). This measure captures the
general concepts of synchronism within the context of rotating machinery. Every SMC has a rotor angle position that is displaced from the
stator AC voltage waveform depending on the power being exported to
the electric grid. See the discussion in Appendix A.2 and Eq. A.2. Because the power output of the machine is determined by the rotor angle,
this is also known as the power angle.

this is also known as the power angle. Following a disturbance, the
rotor angle displacement evolves as expressed by the swing equation, a
rotational kinematic differential equation with rotor angle state variables; see Eq. A.3. When a power system populated with SMCs is synchronized and in steady state, the mechanical (Tm) and electrical (Te)
torques of each SMC are equal in magnitude, and therefore the power

Imbalances between generation from SMCs and load result in deviations from nominal frequency. A decrease in frequency indicates that
generation is insufficient to meet the current load, whereas an increase

3.2. Studying stability with high IBR penetrations
In assessing the stability of a power system, the impacts of a perturbation (such as a load imbalance or fault) on the key stability partitions of voltage, frequency, and rotor angle are typically analyzed. Depending on the size of the power imbalance and the physical influence on the network, there are two fundamentally different approaches
in stability analysis: small-signal and large-signal stability.

customers adjust their power needs, with these types of changes being
relatively small with respect to the total system load. Assessing the
stability during these minor fluctuations is accomplished through a
mathematical framework known as small-signal stability (Kundur,
1994; Van Cutsem and Vournas, 2007). Significant power imbalances
can occur because of a physical change in the network, such as a fault or
the sudden loss of a generator. Such large perturbations result in a

3.2.1. Small-signal stability
Small-signal stability is a method of assessing stability under small
load and/or generation variations without any physical change to the
network. Since there are no physical changes to the network, a mathematical model can be formulated in the form of differential algebraic
equations and linearized to assess the stability around a steady-state
operating point. All dynamic elements are cast in the form of first-order
differential equations using the state-space model, whereas the network
is approximated algebraically by neglecting the electromagnetic transients associated with power transmission.

paper_title: Stability and control of power systems with high penetrations of inverter-based resources_ An accessible review of current knowledge and open questions
text:

is approximated algebraically by neglecting the electromagnetic transients associated with power transmission. When this model is linearized around a steady-state operating point,
a state matrix can be generated and decomposed into eigenvectors and
a diagonal matrix of eigenvalues—the stability of the system can be
determined by the eigenvalues themselves. Generally, a well-defined
system will have an eigenvalue, or pair, associated with a particular
state variable in the system. Participation analysis can be performed to
identify the interplay between various states. Eigenvalues with a negative real part cause a decaying exponential response that goes to zero
over time, which is a general indicator of stability for the affected state. The rate of decay is proportional to the proximity of the eigenvalue real
part to zero.

IBRs differ from centralized SMCs, both in terms of scale as well as
their location on the grid. Whereas most SMCs are connected directly to
the transmission system, a large portion of solar IBRs are connected to
the distribution system as residential rooftop or commercial systems
(Feldman et al., 2020). This distributed generation (DG) is comprised of
many smaller systems rated from just a few to hundreds of kVA, unlike
large transmission-connected assets that are typically tens to hundreds
of MVA (Lin et al., 2017).

whose larger size and/or ownership structure (i.e., utility-, generation

the “utility-scale” label appropriate despite not being directly connected to the transmission system nor reaching the tens of MVA

4.1. Impacts of distributed generation
The presence of DG has both positive and negative impacts on the

4.2. Disturbance response
The operational characteristics of DG during times of abnormal

the power system (Zhu et al., 2018; Kenyon and Mather, 2018). Although these impacts are generally more benign in a low-penetration
scenario, higher penetrations of DG can create a situation in which

grid disturbances (Achilles et al., 2008). The IEEE 1547-2003 standard

5. Simulation and modeling
Bulk power systems are complex, large-scale systems. As a result,
direct experimentation is often not possible, and the field relies heavily
on modeling and simulation for verification and validation of new
ideas. The strategies for simulation and modeling are in a state of
flux–like power systems themselves, which are fundamentally changing
with the rapid growth of new generation technologies such as IBRs. This
section first describes the two major types of simulation used for
studying power system dynamics: RMS and electromagnetic transient
(EMT) simulation. Next, general challenges for meaningful simulation
regardless of type are presented.
5.1. RMS simulation
One common approach for simulating large power systems is to
treat the states of the network (currents and voltages) as steady-state
variables.

text:

One common approach for simulating large power systems is to
treat the states of the network (currents and voltages) as steady-state
variables. In a real power system, voltages and currents are approximately sinusoidal waveforms of a common system frequency. In the
steady-state network approximation, the network states are represented
by a single complex number, typically expressed using phasor notation,
as shown in Fig. 17. The magnitude of the phasor corresponds to the
magnitude of the waveform, and the phase is measured relative to a
reference that is common to the entire network. This simplification
reduces the system to one of algebraic relationships instead of differential equations. When these assumptions are met, an iterative solution
method, such as the Newton-Raphson method, can be employed to
solve for the steady-state load flow.

programs in that voltages and currents are represented in the time

equations rather than algebraic equations (Engineering, 2018).

either present general complications or were historically disregarded. As is typical, such practices were likely suitable at low instantaneous

The most salient feature of DG compared to utility-scale generation
is the number of discrete resources.

In addition to the technical details about the type of simulation
used, there are many practical considerations to ensure useful modeling. In North America, NERC is responsible for developing models
that can be used by industry and researchers. For example, a NERC
working group developed the DER_A modeling framework, which can
be used to model both utility-scale and residential-scale PV far more
effectively than previous attempts (Green, 2019).

and parameterizing the model appropriately, ensuring a common
modeling framework. For models of specific generating plants, regulatory agencies typically rely on models provided by the plant owner. In Australia, concerns
over commercial sensitivity mean that publicly available PSCAD models

5.5. Other modeling challenges
The goal of simulation is often to study system behavior during
faults or other abnormal conditions. Unfortunately, these aspects of a
system are often the most complex and most difficult to model. As
discussed previously, RMS-type simulators are often inadequate in
identifying potential causes of tripping, such as short transient overvoltages, reverse current flow, or loss of PLL synchronism (NERC,
2019b).

overall system dynamics, they can have a profound effect on the system
if they cause an IBR to trip offline. In addition, tripping conditions and

6. Conclusion
The traditional approaches to power system operations are undergoing a transformation as IBR penetrations, both by annual energy and
peak instantaneous power, continue to increase in systems all over the
world. While there are no fundamental hindrances to very high penetrations of IBRs in power systems, they do require amended approaches
to ensure proper stability and operation. The forms these changes need
to take are shaped by the physical differences of SMCs and IBRs. SMC
control and stability is based on the massive, rotational characteristics
of generators, whereas IBRs are built up from power electronic
switches. Because modern power systems were formed around SMCs,
our traditional approaches to stability and control assume large quantities of rotational inertia, which IBRs cannot provide.

Power grids are complex networks consisting of generators, transmission lines, and consumer loads, all designed and operated to transport energy
from the source to consumer. Connecting any two of these three stages (or the intersection of multiple transmission lines) are points known as buses. These systems are run as alternating current (AC), which transmit real (P) and reactive power (Q). Real power, measured in watts (W), is the power
actually delivered to the loads to perform some type of work (i.e. the power consumers pay for, when delivered over a period of time; a watt-hour
(Wh)).

charging and discharging of the inductive and capacitive elements of the system. Below, is a two-bus schematic that includes this system setup and

The frequency of oscillation in the AC power system is electromagnetically linked to the physical rotation of the rotors found in traditional energy
generators, such as coal and nuclear plants. Energy within these generators is harvested through heating pressurised steam and strategically funnelling it to rotate a turbine. This system is called the prime mover. There are typically one or two pole pairs within these turbines that rotate in
synchronous or half-synchronous speeds at 3,600 RPM or 1,800 RPM, respectively, where the number of pole pairs serves to multiple the RPM to the
output frequency.

paper_title: Survey on data-driven control and its application in cyber-physical energy systems
text:
1. Introduction 
1.1. Cyber-physical energy systems 
With the accelerated development of information and communica- 
tion technologies, a critical mass of instruments and devices with com- 
munication functions has been widely deployed in power systems to en- 
hance state observability, control responsiveness, and operational ﬂex- 
ibility in the face of increased penetration of renewable generation at 
all voltage levels and the mass roll-out of electriﬁcation plans across 
many end-user sectors. This trend is transforming energy systems into 
cyber-physical energy systems (CPESs). CPESs tightly integrate power-electrical infrastructure (i.e., gener- 
ation, transmission, and distribution) with layers of sensing, commu- 
nication, and computation to enable real-time monitoring, protection, 
and control of smart grids [1] .

paper_title: Survey on data-driven control and its application in cyber-physical energy systems
text:
distribution) with layers of sensing, commu- 
nication, and computation to enable real-time monitoring, protection, 
and control of smart grids [1] . By fusing energy systems with infor- 
mation and control, CPESs endow physical assets with computation,

precise actuation, coordinated decision-making, and autonomous oper- 
ation, thereby leading to promising improvements in safety, resilience, 
and eﬃciency [2] . Despite these advantages, CPESs pose signiﬁcant challenges to con- 
trol design. First, the underlying physical plants are often highly nonlin- 
ear, time-varying, and only partially known.

paper_title: Survey on data-driven control and its application in cyber-physical energy systems
text:

trol design. First, the underlying physical plants are often highly nonlin- 
ear, time-varying, and only partially known. Second, network-induced 
eﬀects —e.g., communication delays, packet losses, and cybersecurity 
threats — further complicate the realization of reliable and eﬃcient 
control [3,4] . Traditional model-based frameworks (e.g., optimal con- 
trol [5] , robust control [6] , and model predictive control (MPC) [7] ) 
rely on accurate ﬁrst-principles or identiﬁed models, hindering their 
deployment across geographically distributed, heterogeneous CPES in- 
frastructures. Consequently, there is a surging interest in data-driven 
control paradigms, which leverage operational data directly to design 
controllers without full reliance on detailed system models.

1.2. Reinforcement learning based data-driven control 
Whereas many data-driven approaches estimate a map from data 
to control inputs oﬄine, reinforcement learning (RL), a powerful tool 
within the family of machine learning, embeds policy learning within 
the closed-loop interaction, allowing an agent to stochastically explore 
and adapt to its environment online [11] .

text:

the closed-loop interaction, allowing an agent to stochastically explore 
and adapt to its environment online [11] . By formulating power-system 
control tasks as Markov decision processes (MDPs), RL can discover 
adaptive policies that cope with model uncertainty, unmodeled nonlin- 
earities, and evolving operating conditions [12] . In CPESs, RL-based decision mechanisms have attracted intense in- 
terest as a means to overcome the limitations of ﬁxed, model-based con- 
trollers. For example, RL has been applied to voltage regulation [13–15] , 
state estimation [16–18] , energy management [19] , control of power 
converters [20,21] , and economic dispatch [22] . We refer the readers 
to [23] for more references on RL methods applied to CPESs.

converters [20,21] , and economic dispatch [22] . We refer the readers 
to [23] for more references on RL methods applied to CPESs. These 
RL methods have demonstrated the ability to adapt to unforeseen dis- 
turbances and networked interactions that hamper traditional control 
laws, thus representing a powerful complement to model-based designs 
in large-scale, uncertain CPES environments. 
1.3. Willems et al.’s fundamental lemma and direct data-driven control 
Despite the early successes of RL in CPESs, its reliance on large 
amounts of data, signiﬁcant computational resources, and the absence of 
formal stability guarantees limit its deployment in safety-critical infras- 
tructure. In parallel, another data-driven frontier has recently emerged, 
founded on Willems et al.’s fundamental lemma [24] .

paper_title: Survey on data-driven control and its application in cyber-physical energy systems
text:
fety-critical infras- 
tructure. In parallel, another data-driven frontier has recently emerged, 
founded on Willems et al.’s fundamental lemma [24] . This result shows 
that, for a controllable linear time-invariant (LTI) system, a single suf- 
ﬁciently rich input-output trajectory spans the entire system behavior 
via linear combinations of its time-shifts. In eﬀect, one can represent 
all admissible future trajectories with a nonparametric, trajectory-based 
formulation. Inspired by this work, a number of applications and generaliza- 
tions have been developed, including state-feedback and robust control 
[25–29] , data-driven MPC [30–33] , nonlinear system control [34,35] , 
and data-driven state estimation [36–38] .

text:

[25–29] , data-driven MPC [30–33] , nonlinear system control [34,35] , 
and data-driven state estimation [36–38] . Although these techniques are 
still maturing, early applications in CPES contexts —such as data-driven 
voltage regulation, fault detection, and grid synchronization —are al- 
ready emerging [37,39,40] . By circumventing explicit system identi- 
ﬁcation, the fundamental lemma framework promises scalable, theo- 
retically grounded solutions to the high-dimensional, uncertain, and 
network-induced complexities of modern CPESs. 
1.4. Outline of this survey 
The remainder of this survey is organized as follows. Section 6 re- 
views a widely used deep reinforcement learning(DRL) framework.

The remainder of this survey is organized as follows. Section 6 re- 
views a widely used deep reinforcement learning(DRL) framework. Sections 2 –8 then present a comprehensive survey of fundamental 
lemma-based data-driven methods, spanning theoretical developments 
and their potential applications in CPESs. Speciﬁcally, in Section 2 , we 
examine data-driven feedback controller synthesis for LTI systems, cov- 
ering both noise-free and noise-corrupted data scenarios. Section 3 con- 
tinues by exploring recent extensions to nonlinear dynamics, highlight- 
ing key techniques such as lifting, immersion, and interpolation. In 
Section 4 , we introduce data-driven predictive-control architectures, 
with particular emphasis on robust formulations and the explicit han- 
dling of measurement noise.

paper_title: Survey on data-driven control and its application in cyber-physical energy systems
text:
duce data-driven predictive-control architectures, 
with particular emphasis on robust formulations and the explicit han- 
dling of measurement noise. Section 5 surveys advances in data-driven 
state estimation, focusing on nonparametric and learning-based ob- 
server designs. Section 8 presents representative CPES applications, 
demonstrating how the discussed methods can be deployed in real-world 
grid settings. Finally, Section 9 synthesizes the key insights from this 
survey and outlines promising directions for future research. Through this structured overview, we aim to demonstrate how data- 
driven control, anchored in recent theoretical advances, can address the 
grand challenges facing next-generation cyber-physical energy infras- 
tructures. 
1.5. Notation 
Throughout the paper, we adhere to a standard set of notations, 
which are detailed in Table 1 for clarity and reference.

2. Data-driven feedback control for LTI systems 
To provide a solid foundation for tackling more complex problems, 
this section focuses on the essential model class of LTI systems. Our goal 
is to control such systems using pre-collected measurement data. We 
begin by introducing a basic data-driven framework that utilizes exact 
(noise-free) and measured (noisy) input-state data, followed by imple- 
mentations based on noise-free and noisy input-output data. Finally, we 
review applications of this approach in addressing several classic prob- 
lems in control theory.

Sections 2.2 – 2.3 presented basic data-driven design frameworks un-

is related strongly to the traditional control theory. Hence, several ef-

In this section, we reviewed a suite of fundamental lemma-based

2.5. Summary and outlook 
In this section, we reviewed a suite of fundamental lemma-based 
methods for data-driven feedback control of LTI systems. Starting from 
exact input-state trajectories, we demonstrated how to compute state- 
feedback gains via a data-dependent LMI. We then extended these re- 
sults to accommodate noisy input-state data through slack variables and 
robust formulations. Next, we relaxed the requirement for state mea- 
surements by employing input-output data and further addressed mea- 
surement noise with regularization techniques. Finally, we surveyed sev- 
eral important extensions, including optimal control, online implemen- 
tation, robust control, dissipativity, distributed control and aperiodic 
control.

control. Together, these developments show that fundamental lemma-based 
controllers can recover classical objectives, e.g., stability, optimality, 
and robustness, in a fully data-driven fashion. However, their inher- 
ent reliance on linear dynamics limits applicability in CPES components 
with strong nonlinear behavior. This motivates the transition in the next

3.4. Extensions 
Besides methods reviewed in Sections 3.2 and 3.3 , recent work 
has linked nonlinear data-driven systems with linear parameter-varying 
(LPV) systems [85] , input-to-state stability (ISS) analysis [86] , and state- 
dependent representations [87] . Compared with numerous eﬀorts made 
in the LTI case in Section 2.4 , many avenues remain open for future ex- 
ploration. 
3.5. Summary and outlook 
In this section, we reviewed nonlinear data-driven feedback control 
based on the representation 𝑥𝑘 +1 = 𝐴 𝑍( 𝑥𝑘 ) + 𝐵 𝑢𝑘 , treating separately 
the cases where the embedding 𝑍( 𝑥 ) is known and where it must be 
learned from data.

section: 3. Data-driven feedback control for nonlinear systems
paper_title: Survey on data-driven control and its application in cyber-physical energy systems
text:
representation 𝑥𝑘 +1 = 𝐴 𝑍( 𝑥𝑘 ) + 𝐵 𝑢𝑘 , treating separately 
the cases where the embedding 𝑍( 𝑥 ) is known and where it must be 
learned from data. So far, we have covered fundamental lemma-style 
state feedback methods for both LTI and nonlinear systems. However, 
these methods are inherently limited to instantaneous feedback and lack 
built-in mechanisms for multi-step prediction and explicit constraint 
handling —capabilities essential to many CPES applications. To address 
these limitations, the next section turns to data-driven model predic- 
tive control (MPC), which embeds data-based system representations in 
a ﬁnite-horizon optimization framework to provide foresight, enforce 
constraints, and optimize performance over future trajectories.

paper_title: Survey on data-driven control and its application in cyber-physical energy systems
text:
4. Data-driven predictive control 
The previous sections introduced data-driven feedback controllers 
for both LTI and nonlinear systems. In traditional control theory, model 
predictive control (MPC) plays a central role due to its ability to han- 
dle multivariable systems, explicitly incorporate constraints, and opti- 
mize system performance over a prediction horizon. Its eﬀectiveness 
has been widely demonstrated in diverse real-world applications, rang- 
ing from industrial chemical process control, where safety and eﬃciency 
are paramount, to high-precision tasks such as UAV trajectory tracking 
[88] , where dynamic environments and physical limitations must be ac- 
counted for in real time. Therefore, in contrast to the feedback control 
methods discussed earlier, another popular research direction is the ap- 
plication of data-driven approaches to MPC.

4.3. Extensions 
Extensions in this literature have been made including self-triggered 
control [32,33] , resilient control [31] , nonlinear tracking [91] , dis- 
tributed control [92] , min-max MPC [93] , stochasic setting [94,95] , 
complex network [96] , and implementations in real-world quadcopter 
[97] . 
4.4. Summary and outlook 
In this section, we reviewed data-driven MPC using Willems’ funda- 
mental lemma, covering both the nominal noise-free formulation and 
robust variants with slack variables and regularization.

paper_title: Survey on data-driven control and its application in cyber-physical energy systems
text:
PC using Willems’ funda- 
mental lemma, covering both the nominal noise-free formulation and 
robust variants with slack variables and regularization. Key extensions 
include self-triggered, resilient, nonlinear, distributed, and stochastic 
schemes, as well as real-world implementations. While these methods 
oﬀer powerful data-driven control solutions for CPESs, accurate state es- 
timation remains essential for reliable monitoring, fault detection, and 
higher-level decision-making under partial observability. To address this 
need, the next section surveys data-driven state estimation techniques 
that reconstruct internal states directly from measured data.

real-world systems [98] . This section reviews recent advances in data-

5.2. Summary and outlook 
In this ﬁnal section of the fundamental lemma-based frame- 
work, we reviewed data-driven state estimation methods that recon- 
struct system states from oﬄine input-state-output datasets and on- 
line measurements without explicit models.

paper_title: Survey on data-driven control and its application in cyber-physical energy systems
text:
state estimation methods that recon- 
struct system states from oﬄine input-state-output datasets and on- 
line measurements without explicit models. Taken together with earlier 
developments —data-driven feedback controller synthesis for LTI sys- 
tems ( Section 2 ), nonlinear systems ( Section 3 ), and data-driven MPC 
( Section 4 ) —these methods oﬀer rigorous stability, performance, and 
robustness guarantees under speciﬁc structural assumptions. However, 
these assumptions are often violated in highly complex or uncertain 
CPES environments. To address such scenarios, the next section turns 
to purely model-free DRL approaches, which learn control policies di- 
rectly from interaction data without any structural prerequisites.

DRL is a prominent machine learning paradigm, which combines the

6.2. DRL in CPES 
In cyber-physical energy systems, DRL oﬀers a distinct advantage 
over traditional optimization and control techniques by enabling sys- 
tems to learn optimal policies through continuous interaction with com- 
plex and uncertain environments. This capability is particularly well- 
suited to the dynamic, distributed, and data-intensive characteristics of 
modern energy systems. As CPES increasingly integrates renewable en- 
ergy sources, energy storage, and advanced digital control mechanisms, 
DRL has emerged as a powerful tool to enhance system ﬂexibility, re- 
silience, and operational eﬃciency.

6.3. Summary and outlook 
In summary, DRL provides a fully model-free framework for tack- 
ling high-dimensional, nonlinear CPES control tasks — such as voltage 
regulation under uncertainty — by learning policies directly from in- 
teraction data. However, both DRL and the fundamental lemma-based 
data-driven methods reviewed earlier assume that online measurements 
and control commands are reliable and untampered. In practice, CPES 
networks are vulnerable to adversarial cyber-physical attacks that can 
corrupt or block these data streams.

7.1. DoS attacks 
DoS attacks are designed to disrupt data availability, typically by 
jamming or ﬂooding communication channels with malicious traﬃc 
[120] . In CPESs, such interruptions may occur along (i) the link between 
remote terminal units (RTUs) or phasor measurement units (PMUs) and 
the control center, and (ii) the link between the control center and gener- 
ator governors. By blocking measurement updates or delaying actuator 
commands, DoS attacks can severely degrade system performance and 
precipitate instability. In what follows, we ﬁrst review data-driven detection methods and 
then turn to resilient control strategies.

7.1.1. Detection via RL 
As a strong technique in obtaining optimal action policies in diﬀer- 
ent domains, RL approaches have shown promise in learning optimal 
detection and mitigation policies under varying DoS scenarios: 
• DRL framework: [131] developed a DRL-based framework that 
learned to mitigate distributed DoS ﬂooding in real time by dynam- 
ically adapting its policy to evolving attack patterns. 
• Model-free RL for POMDPs: [122] cast the DoS detection problem as a 
partially observable markov decision process (POMDPs) and applied 
model-free RL to derive a robust, universal detection algorithm. 
• Recursive CNN-enhanced Q-learning: [123] proposed an anti-jamming 
algorithm using Q-learning with a recursive convolutional neural 
network to extract temporal features from spectrum-waterfall data 
for enhanced detection.

7.3. Extensions 
While the preceding subsections have surveyed data-driven detec- 
tion and resilient control techniques for DoS and FDI attacks individ- 
ually, real-world adversaries may deploy coordinated [155] or hybrid 
attack [156] strategies that interleave multiple attack vectors to evade 
single-mode countermeasures. For instance, an attacker might brieﬂy 
ﬂood communication channels (which is a type of DoS attacks) to force 
the system into open-loop operation, then inject stealthy false data (FDI) 
into the next available measurement batch to maximize disruption. To extend our resilient control framework to such compound threats, 
we propose the following directions: 
1.

easurement batch to maximize disruption. To extend our resilient control framework to such compound threats, 
we propose the following directions: 
1. Composite detection architectures. Fuse DoS detectors (e.g., RL-based 
jamming classiﬁers in Section 7.1 ) with FDI residual and funda- 
mental lemma detectors (cf. Section 7.2 ) into a uniﬁed anomaly- 
scoring mechanism. By jointly monitoring packet arrival patterns 
and feature-space consistency, the system can identify hybrid sig- 
natures, such as synchronized packet losses and small, correlated 
measurement shifts, that would bypass isolated detectors. 
2. Adaptive slack-variable design. Building on the robust predictive con- 
trol of Section 4 , introduce attack-mode-dependent slack variables 
in the MPC formulation.

trol of Section 4 , introduce attack-mode-dependent slack variables 
in the MPC formulation. During detected DoS intervals, slack vari- 
ables compensate for missing measurements, while under FDI suspi- 
cions they adaptively tighten bounds on predicted outputs. A coher- 
ent slack-scheduling policy ensures feasibility across attack phases 
and preserves performance when returning to nominal operation. 
3. Mode-switching control policies. Leverage the ADP-based resilient reg-

switch between high-performance and conservative controllers. Upon detecting a hybrid attack sequence, transition to a conser- 
vative, low-gain controller that prioritizes stability and safety over 
tracking accuracy, then revert once the attack ceases.

vative, low-gain controller that prioritizes stability and safety over

4. Resilience metrics and benchmarking. Deﬁne quantitative metrics that 
capture end-to-end CPES performance under sequential or over- 
lapping DoS-FDI scenarios (e.g., availability loss, estimation error 
growth, recovery time). Establish standardized simulation bench- 
marks, to evaluate and compare future defense schemes under hy- 
brid threats. By integrating detection and control adaptations across both DoS and 
FDI dimensions, and by introducing attack-aware slack scheduling and 
mode-switching policies, the extended framework will better mirror the 
complexity of emerging cyber-physical attacks and oﬀer practitioners

7.3.1. Summary and outlook 
In this section, we surveyed data-driven strategies for detecting and 
mitigating DoS and FDI attacks in CPESs. Detection methods ranged 
from RL-based jamming classiﬁers to adaptive residual and fundamen- 
tal lemma monitors, while resilient control schemes included predic- 
tive controllers with slack variables, ADP-based regulation, and time- 
varying feedback laws. We also proposed extensions for coordinated or 
hybrid attacks via composite detectors, attack-aware slack scheduling, 
and mode-switching policies. Building on these developments, the next 
section presents real-world CPES applications to illustrate the practical 
performance of the reviewed control, estimation, and security methods.

8. Applications in CPESs 
Rapidly rising energy demand and growing environmental concerns 
have spurred the integration of renewables, eﬃciency measures, storage 
solutions, and demand-side management into modern power systems. CPESs, which seamlessly fuse energy-process dynamics with sensing, 
communication, and real-time computation, oﬀer a promising platform 
for addressing the uncertainties of renewable generation and the oper- 
ational challenges of large, geographically distributed grids. To thrive 
under future stresses, CPESs must exhibit adaptivity across multiple di- 
mensions: ﬂexibility to accommodate variable generation and load; ef- 
ﬁciency in resource utilization; sustainability in emissions and resource 
use; reliability under component failures or disturbances; and security 
against cyber threats.

8.2. Two-area load frequency control 
In Section 8.1 , we developed a prototype data-driven design for the 
simplest single-machine model. We now extend these ideas to the clas- 
sical two-area load frequency control (LFC) problem, showcasing how 
direct data-driven controllers can address its inherent challenges. Large-scale power systems are naturally partitioned into intercon- 
nected control areas.

paper_title: Survey on data-driven control and its application in cyber-physical energy systems
text:
data-driven controllers can address its inherent challenges. Large-scale power systems are naturally partitioned into intercon- 
nected control areas. Within each area, LFC must maintain both the local 
frequency and the power exchanged over the tie-line as close as possi- 
ble to their scheduled setpoints. The mechanical input power to each 
generator is adjusted to balance load changes and regulate inter-area 
power ﬂows. In modern deregulated markets, each control area faces 
signiﬁcant uncertainties, ranging from load variations to modeling mis- 
matches and evolving network structures, while still requiring tight fre- 
quency regulation and high power quality under voltage and frequency 
constraints. Fig. 7 depicts two areas linked by a tie-line: each area serves a lo- 
cal load, and tie-line power deviations reveal inter-area imbalances.

voltage trajectories under data-driven predictive control were notably 
smoother.

output data.

9. Conclusions 
In this survey, we have chronicled the rapid evolution of data- 
driven control for CPESs, beginning with nonparametric, trajectory- 
44 W. Liu, M. Zhang, Q. Xu et al. Cyber-Physical Energy Systems 1 (2025) 28–48
based methods grounded in Willems et al.’s fundamental lemma. We ﬁrst 
detailed how these methods —requiring an LTI or suitably lifted system 
representation —enable state-feedback synthesis in linear and nonlinear 
settings, extend naturally to model predictive control, and support non- 
parametric state estimation under both noise-free and noisy conditions. We then reviewed RL approaches, which lift structural constraints en- 
tirely and learn control policies directly from interaction data, trading 
formal stability proofs for broad applicability to complex and uncertain 
grid dynamics.

paper_title: Survey on data-driven control and its application in cyber-physical energy systems
text:
arn control policies directly from interaction data, trading 
formal stability proofs for broad applicability to complex and uncertain 
grid dynamics. Building on these control and estimation foundations, 
we turned to CPES-speciﬁc challenges by surveying data-driven defense 
strategies against DoS and FDI attacks, from anomaly detection to re- 
silient controller design. Finally, to illustrate practical impact, we ex- 
amined a series of case studies, from canonical generator benchmarks 
to high-ﬁdelity, grid-connected wind-turbine simulations, showcasing 
how both trajectory-based controllers and RL agents can meet the scale, 
complexity, and uncertainties of modern power networks. Looking ahead, several research avenues stand out as particularly 
fertile: 
• Learning-augmented data-driven methods.

paper_title: Survey on data-driven control and its application in cyber-physical energy systems
text:
nties of modern power networks. Looking ahead, several research avenues stand out as particularly 
fertile: 
• Learning-augmented data-driven methods. By embedding RL 
[23,160] or other learning agents around fundamental lemma- 
based inner loops, one can leverage live operational data to 
reﬁne policies or value functions while retaining provable sta- 
bility and performance certiﬁcates. Such hybrid schemes hold 
promise for large-scale, time-varying CPES tasks, i.e., from load- 
frequency regulation to voltage security, oﬀering faster adaptation 
under nonstationary conditions without sacriﬁcing theoretical 
rigor. 
• Core CPES control problems. Although foundational tasks such as volt- 
age regulation and frequency stabilization have been addressed us- 
ing RL-based data-driven approaches [161] , they remain ripe for fun- 
damental lemma-based data-driven treatment.

paper_title: Survey on data-driven control and its application in cyber-physical energy systems
text:
bilization have been addressed us- 
ing RL-based data-driven approaches [161] , they remain ripe for fun- 
damental lemma-based data-driven treatment. Tailoring reviewed 
data-driven methods to these canonical power-system challenges 
promises both theoretical insight and tangible operational beneﬁts 
[162] . 
• Network-induced phenomena. Beyond the cyber-threats we have re- 
viewed in Section 7 , CPESs also face with communication delays, 
packet drops, and topology changes. Extending data-driven tools, 
especially those inherently robust to aperiodic sampling or adver- 
sarial data, to these settings will further enhance grid resilience and 
security. 
• Topology inference and integration. The geographically distributed na- 
ture of CPESs gives rise to complex interaction networks.

paper_title: Survey on data-driven control and its application in cyber-physical energy systems
text:
ce and 
security. 
• Topology inference and integration. The geographically distributed na- 
ture of CPESs gives rise to complex interaction networks. Recent 
causality-based methods proposed in [163] can infer network topol- 
ogy from a single trajectory, providing valuable insight into system 
behavior. Integrating topology inference with data-driven control 
promises to improve performance by tailoring algorithms to the true 
underlying structure. 
• Optimization integration. Beyond real-time control and estimation, 
CPES operation hinges on solving large optimization problems, such 
as optimal power ﬂow [164] , economic dispatch [22] , and demand 
response [165] . Embedding nonparametric, data-driven plant mod- 
els into convex or distributed optimization frameworks promises to 
accelerate decision-making and improve scalability. 
• Bridging theory and practice.

paper_title: Survey on data-driven control and its application in cyber-physical energy systems
text:
s into convex or distributed optimization frameworks promises to 
accelerate decision-making and improve scalability. 
• Bridging theory and practice. While countless algorithms have 
been born in simulation, real-world validation on e.g., hardware 
testbeds, microgrids, or utility pilots, remains urgent. Deploying 
data-driven controllers in these environments will expose practi- 
cal issues of robustness, computational tractability, and legacy- 
system interoperability, thereby closing the loop between theory and 
application. By pursuing these directions, the control community can not only 
deepen the theoretical foundations of data-driven methods but also de- 
liver the adaptive, resilient, and eﬃcient solutions that tomorrow’s en- 
ergy systems demand.

1. Introduction
The future of the global energy system is deeply uncertain, and the choices that 
are made in the coming years will have enormous consequences for the future of 
the climate and, indeed, human civilization. To understand how our energy system 
is changing, each year a variety of organizations produce long-term projections 
that imagine a wide range of futures based on divergent visions about policies, 
technologies, prices, and geopolitics. Because these projections vary widely and depend heavily on their varied assumptions 
and methodologies, they are difficult to compare on an apples-to-apples basis. In this 
report, we apply a detailed harmonization process to compare 16 scenarios across 
eight energy outlooks published in 2023, as well as two historical data sources.

2. Key Findings
At the 28th Conference of the Parties (COP28) to the United Nations Framework 
Convention on Climate Change held in Dubai, world leaders agreed to “transitioning 
away from fossil fuels in the energy system.”11 Some advocates, governments, and 
civil society figures have critiqued this agreement and argued instead for the total 
phaseout of fossil fuels to achieve long-term climate goals. However, all scenarios 
examined here, including those consistent with limiting warming to 1.5°C by 2100, show 
substantial global fossil fuel consumption through at least 2050, suggesting that a 
phaseout is not a prerequisite to achieving international climate goals.

tial global fossil fuel consumption through at least 2050, suggesting that a 
phaseout is not a prerequisite to achieving international climate goals. As we have noted in previous Global Energy Outlooks,12 world primary energy demand 
has experienced a series of energy additions, not energy transitions, with newer 
technologies such as nuclear, wind, and solar building on top of incumbent sources 
such as biomass, coal, oil, and natural gas. To achieve international climate goals and 
limit warming to 1.5°C or 2°C by 2100, a true energy transition is needed. But does 
achieving such goals require phasing out fossil fuels entirely? The scenarios we analyze in this report suggest that the answer is no.

If fossil fuels are not phased out of the energy system, limiting warming to international 
climate targets implies a substantial scale-up of carbon removal technologies, including 
direct air capture (DAC), bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (CCS), and naturebased solutions, all of which will require robust monitoring, reporting, and verification.

scale is an essential tool in reaching net-zero emissions in every Ambitious Climate scenario 
examined here. In 2022, roughly 42 million metric tons of CO2 were captured by CCUS infrastructure around

represents a near tripling of CCUS since 2010, a compound average annual growth rate

As the global economy becomes more energy efficient, world primary energy demand 
grows slowly or declines under almost all scenarios examined here. This trend is seen 
most clearly in Ambitious Climate scenarios, where aggregate energy demand declines 
by as much as 33 percent (Equinor Bridges). Falling energy demand occurs primarily in 
high-income countries, with continued growth in energy consumption in many low-income 
nations. Some scenarios, such as the IEA’s NZE, highlight how expanding access to modern 
energy services in low-income regions can be consistent with declining global energy 
demand and achieving long-term sustainability goals.

remained roughly flat, declining modestly from 2010 through today. In the decades

need for enhanced policy ambition if nations are to achieve their COP28 renewable 
energy goals. In 2010, renewable electricity was dominated by hydropower, which accounted 
for more than 75 percent of installed capacity worldwide.

the United States, Asia, and the Middle East. Unlike coal and oil, which peak under 
most scenarios examined here, natural gas demand increases under roughly half of 
the scenarios. This divergence highlights the complex role that natural gas plays in

Philippines, Russia, New Caledonia, and Australia.55 Indonesia is also the world’s largest 
nickel processor, at 43 percent of the global total, followed by China at 17 percent.49

3.3.5. Other Minerals
Although the four minerals discussed in the previous subsections are some of the 
most significant in terms of scale, their rate of clean energy–related demand growth 
is dwarfed by that of other clean energy minerals (Figure 21). While demand for 
lithium grows by roughly one order of magnitude under most of the bp, IEA, and 
Shell scenarios, demand for gallium—which is used in semiconductors and other 
electronics—rises by nearly three orders of magnitude by 2040 under IEA’s scenarios. Demand for vanadium, which today is used in specialized steelmaking and other 
industrial applications, grows fastest in all these scenarios, rising by nearly five orders 
of magnitude by 2040.

industrial applications, grows fastest in all these scenarios, rising by nearly five orders 
of magnitude by 2040. Unlike copper and nickel, which have been mined at scale for generations, many 
clean energy minerals are starting from a very small base, which helps explain their 
extraordinary rates of growth. For example, the USGS reports that global production of 
gallium in 2022 was roughly 550 metric tons,56 less than 2 percent of which were used 
in clean energy.49 Similarly, global vanadium production in 2022 was 100,000 metric 
tons,57 roughly 0.1 percent of which was used in clean energy.49 By 2050, clean energy–
driven demand for gallium reaches 3,300 metric tons under the IEA’s STEPS, six times 
today’s global production across all sectors.

4.  Data and Methods
In this paper, we examined projections energy outlooks from a wide range of sources 
representing a diverse set of views on the future of energy (see Table 1).

assumes no major policy changes; (2) Evolving Policies, which incorporates the 
modeling team’s expectations of policy trends; and (3) scenarios that do not fall into 
one of the other two categories and are typically based on policy targets or technology 
assumptions. We focus on Ambitious Climate scenarios, a major subset of category 3.

4.1. Harmonization
Variations in underlying assumptions about the future of policies, technologies, 
and markets produce useful variation among outlooks, allowing analysts to view 
a wide range of potential energy futures. However, outlooks also have important 
methodological differences, which can complicate direct comparisons and reduce the 
ability to draw insights. One major difference is the choice of reporting units. For primary energy, outlooks 
use different energy units, such as QBtu, million tonnes of oil equivalent (mtoe), 
or exajoules (EJ). In this report, we standardize all units to QBtu.

A second key difference among outlooks is that assumptions about the energy content 
in a given physical unit of fuel result in different conversion factors between data 
presented in energy units (e.g., QBtu) and those presented in physical units (e.g., mbd 
or bcm). Among the outlooks we examine, these assumptions vary by up to 10 percent. Although conversion unit variations may appear small, they are amplified when applied 
across the massive scale of global energy systems, particularly over long time horizons. A third major difference results from varying decisions about including nonmarketed 
biomass, such as locally gathered wood and dung, in historical data and projections 
for primary energy consumption.

ions about including nonmarketed 
biomass, such as locally gathered wood and dung, in historical data and projections 
for primary energy consumption. In previous years, bp and the EIA had not included 
these sources in their projections. However, bp’s Energy Outlook 2023 does include 
nonmarketed biomass, allowing for enhanced comparability. (The EIA publishes its 
International Energy Outlook every two years and did not publish one in 2023.) 
Yet another difference relates to comparing the energy content of fossil and 
nonfossil fuels. The primary energy content of oil, natural gas, and coal is relatively 
well understood and similar across outlooks. However, a substantial portion of that 
embodied energy is wasted as heat during combustion.

variety of approaches. Other differences in outlooks include (1) different categorizations for liquid fuels and

(3) using net versus gross calorific values when reporting energy content of fossil fuels, 
(4) using net versus gross generation when reporting electricity data, and (5) whether 
and how flared natural gas is included in energy consumption data.

paper_title: Grid Forming Converters for Low Inertia Systems-Capabilities and Limitations: A Critical Review
text:
ABSTRACT
The rapid integration of renewable energy sources into the power grid has resulted in the
high utilization of power-electronics devices and operating power systems where inverter-based resources
are dominated. Such a transition has led to a reduction of inertia and system strength. In recent research,
grid-forming converters (GFM) are introduced and developed to alleviate the grid-following converter (GFL)
functionalities and to address the limitations concerning grid support capability, stability, and synchronization
issues. However, the efﬁcacy of GFM technology is still under investigation, and the level at which GFM
converters can replace traditional GFLs is still under question.

paper_title: Grid Forming Converters for Low Inertia Systems-Capabilities and Limitations: A Critical Review
text:
he efﬁcacy of GFM technology is still under investigation, and the level at which GFM
converters can replace traditional GFLs is still under question. This article aims to bridge the gap in
literature by revisiting the up-to-date research on the capabilities and the limitations of the proposed GFM
converters compared to the traditionally utilized GFL converters, allowing a better understanding of the
current status and future requirements. This includes the GFM converter’s topologies and their performance
for small- and large-signal stability issues, the GFM converters’ ability to enhance grid synchronization,
and transient stability performances.

for small- and large-signal stability issues, the GFM converters’ ability to enhance grid synchronization,
and transient stability performances. Furthermore, the challenges and limitations of the dynamic behavior
of GFM converters from the point of view of fault ride through (FRT) capability, including grid codes and
FRT requirements, FRT methods of GFM converters, postfault behavior, and open research directions, are
also comprehensively reviewed. Finally, this article has been concluded by highlighting the main ﬁndings,
considerations, and future recommendations.

II. GFM CONTROL METHODS
In this section, the most common control concepts of the GFM
converter are revised based on their structure, importance,
issues, and enhancements in recent years. These control concepts are divided into two major groups: droop control and SM
control. The GFM converter control should be able to operate
accurately in low system strength conditions, stabilize grid
voltage and frequency, and resynchronize with the grid after
the occurrence of the disturbance. In addition, FRT capability,
system restoration, and black-start capability are required to
be improved when the fault occurs [37].

text:
III. CHALLENGES AND LIMITATIONS OF GFM
CONVERTERS
GFM converters are a potential solution for RESs integration
to avoid the stability issues in weak inertial grids compared to
the GFL converters. This is due to their superior capabilities,
such as enhanced synchronization in weak systems, black start
capability, and ROCOF capability. However, recent research
has raised modern challenges such as high grid impedance,
lower SCR, and lower inertia [109]. In these subsections, the
small signal stability, transient stability, and postfault recovery
have been considered. The saturation of the current limiter is
another problem that has been raised [110], and it is solved by
utilizing the virtual impedance-based voltage limiting strategy
covered in these subsections. Grid strength affects the GFM
performances, stability, and performance, either in weak or
strong grid conditions.

and let the nadir frequency oscillate outside the acceptable
limit.

3) POSTFAULT STABILITY (VOLTAGE RECOVERY)
Fault protection is a crucial component in GFM converters,
and installation is required to protect the GFM converters
from high current levels during short-circuit events. The effectiveness depends on several factors, such as the clearance
time under frequency and voltage disturbances, SCR conditions, and postfault stability. The ideal fault protection scheme
should operate under different fault types and all SCR conditions and have an instantaneous response to a fault [68].

C. FRT CAPABILITY
Several disturbances occur in the power grid, such as transmission faults and tripping of large generators, resulting in
electromagnetic transient and triggering system-level problems. FRT capability or voltage-ride-through or disturbance
ride-through is introduced and deﬁned in [167] as the ability
of the inverter-based generation to withstand abnormal transients and remain connected. This section focuses on the FRT
capability, considering the available grid codes, requirements,
and shortages.
1) GRID CODES AND FRT REQUIREMENTS
The output currents of GFM converters not only depend on
the external system condition but also on the FRT behavior, the internal settings, and the overrating capability of the
converter itself [168].

paper_title: Grid Forming Converters for Low Inertia Systems-Capabilities and Limitations: A Critical Review
text:
end on
the external system condition but also on the FRT behavior, the internal settings, and the overrating capability of the
converter itself [168]. While synchronous generators can supply 5–7 per unit (p.u.) overcurrent during disturbances at the
PCC, the inverters may supply up to 2 p.u. overcurrent [169]. This would allow the inverters to contribute to the dynamic
voltage support to maintain the voltage proﬁle and achieve
a smooth voltage recovery. Proper FRT strategies, including
current limiting methods, are necessary for GFM converters
to provide such supporting functionality during disturbances. Thus, the following requirements have to be achieved [170]:
1) current magnitude limitation;
2) fault current contribution;
3) fault recovery capability.

paper_title: Grid Forming Converters for Low Inertia Systems-Capabilities and Limitations: A Critical Review
text:

1) current magnitude limitation;
2) fault current contribution;
3) fault recovery capability. The GFM converters can meet these requirements by employing a proper control mechanism equipped with distinct
current limiting control methods. Virtual impedance, current
limiters, and voltage limiters are the most common methods
in the literature for current limiting by GFM converters. The necessity of meeting such requirements may increase
with the increased penetration of power electronic converters
in the systems, which imposes technical challenges on the
power network, especially if these converters do not emulate
the behavior of the SM. In this regard, other settings and grid
code requirements might be necessary.

requirements for GFM speciﬁcations discussed in a draft for
Great Britain was determined as the following [171].
1) The GFM converter has to operate like a voltage source
connected with a reactance and the frequency band
should be between 5 Hz–1 kHz during, before and after
the fault condition.
2) The contribution of the short-circuit current of the GFM
converter has to be 1.5 p.u. from its rating. This value is
a compromise between the preferable overcurrent capability of a SM and the hardware constraints.
3) The voltage magnitude, frequency, and phase angle of
the GFM converter shall remain ﬁxed at pre-fault values
during a voltage dip or fault below 0.85 p.u.

4) The GFM converter has to be able to inject reactive

The literature has extensively addressed the FRT control

signiﬁcant increase in research addressing this gap, leading to

IV. CONCLUSION
Since GFM converters are crucial in operating modern power
grids in stable and reliable operation, this article comprehensively reviewed a GFM converter structure and working
principles. Various GFM control methods have been comprehensively revised in terms of the structure, importance, issues,
and enhancements in recent years. It was concluded that the
GFM converter control be able to operate accurately in low
system strength conditions, ensuring stable operation of both
voltage and frequency. However, this fact becomes inaccurate
for some speciﬁc conditions of the power network. Therefore, this article highlights the challenges and limitations of
the GFM converter with an increase of RESs’ penetration
level. Also, the performance of the GFM converter, considering the grid strength, was reviewed.

3 Grid forming control design
With the rapid development of wind power worldwide,
the unique characteristics of wind power’s static and
dynamic responses have emerged new major challenges related to the adequacy and stability of the
modern power system. One of the prominent concerns regarding the increasing penetration of wind
power is its impact on power system frequency stability due to the lack of positive response from the installed WTs to frequency disturbances, i.e., large load
ﬂuctuations or generating unit losses occurring in the
power grid [9].

ive response from the installed WTs to frequency disturbances, i.e., large load
ﬂuctuations or generating unit losses occurring in the
power grid [9]. Therefore, the dynamic frequency support capability of wind power will be much needed in
the near future to ensure that frequency stability is
not compromised. It is known that almost all of the
installed WTs currently are adopting the typical vector control method based on the phase-locked-loop
(PLL) synchronizing technique. The PLL performs
well for a strong grid where the grid dictates voltage angle magnitudes to the controls of the WT’s converter. Such an arrangement where converter controls
follow the voltage angle and voltage magnitude inputs
from a strong grid and behave as a current source is
known as a grid-following (GFL) control strategy. K

and loss of synchronization during weak-grid and grid fault
conditions [3]–[5]. Furthermore, with a trend for connecting
generation at all voltage levels and with a future possibility
for islanded operation of different parts of the network as

functionalities of synchronous machines including the provision of synthetic inertia and a power-based synchronization
mechanism. Among the grid-forming converters, numerous control

magnitude and frequency set-point but modify these based

converters may also be referred to as grid-supporting gridforming converters [17]. It should be noted that grid-following

transient characteristics and fault behavior, as replicating the
short-circuit behavior of a synchronous machine is not feasible
with current-sensitive semiconductor devices. As described in [17], [18], there are mainly two methods
which can provide current limitation and stability for gridforming converter under large-signal disturbances: switching
the control structure to the grid-following mode during the
fault and limiting the converter currents using a virtual admittance structure.

the control structure to the grid-following mode during the
fault and limiting the converter currents using a virtual admittance structure. Along these lines, in [19], the converter control
is switched to hysteresis control if the permissible allowed
current is being exceeded. This method obviously loses all
functionalities of the grid-forming control during this period,
and how to deal with the saturation of outer control loops is
not discussed. In a similar fashion, switching to grid-following
control during the fault is proposed in [14], [20]–[22]. This
solution needs a backup PLL for the synchronization, which
then has its own stability issues for weak-grid conditions. As previously shown, the current limitation can be achieved
simply by limiting the current references directly during the
fault.

text:

simply by limiting the current references directly during the
fault. However, this will cause wind-up in the outer power
loops, which can lead to instability [17]. To circumvent this,
several researchers propose the use of virtual resistors, either
linear [23] or nonlinear [24] to reduce the converter voltage
reference. Also, the inﬂuence of a virtual impedance structure
on the current limitation is analyzed in [25]. As disclosed,
the current limitation is largely depending on the fault location
and the selected virtual impedance, which may limit its
usefulness in practice as the maximum converter current is
desired to be utilized during any fault condition. To that end,
the virtual impedance concept may cause problems in parallel
operation [24].

desired to be utilized during any fault condition. To that end,
the virtual impedance concept may cause problems in parallel
operation [24]. In [26], both limitations of the inner current
reference and voltage reference reduction using the virtual
impedance concept are conducted. In this way, the currents
are limited and wind-up in the outer loops are avoided
using the virtual impedance concept. Nevertheless, the virtual
impedance still has the problem that its accuracy of limitation
depends on several unknown factors as previously mentioned. Conclusively, for the methods that switch to a grid-following
structure during the fault, the robust grid-forming properties
of the converter are lost. To that end, for the methods that
directly limit the current references, either the outer power
loops and droop controllers are not considered or wind-up
and instability is encountered.

loops and droop controllers are not considered or wind-up
and instability is encountered. To avoid wind-up in the outer
power loops while limiting the currents, a virtual impedance
may be used. However, the limiting performance of this is
variable and depends on several unknown factors, which makes
the utilization of it less attractive. Hence, how to deal with
saturation in the outer loops alongside how to sustain the
grid-forming structure while limiting the converter currents
is not well described in the available literature. Thereby, this
article aims to describe the issues of the current limitation of
grid-forming converters considering the outer loops and their
inﬂuence on the converter response.
